channel.title: Aggregated External AI & Tech News
channel.description: Merged headlines from configured external sources

item.title: Ars Asks: Share your shell and show us your tricked-out terminals! (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: A celebration of the tweaks and customizations that make life easier at the CLI.

item.title: Mozilla says 271 vulnerabilities found by Mythos have "almost no false positives" (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: The developer of Firefox says it has "completely bought in" on AI-assisted bug discovery.

item.title: Chaos erupts as cyberattack disrupts learning platform Canvas amid finals (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Across the country, schools and colleges postpone year-end tests.

item.title: Linux bitten by second severe vulnerability in as many weeks (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Production-version patches are coming online and should be installed pronto.

item.title: Cisco announces record revenue and 4,000 layoffs in the same day (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Layoffs are "not a savings-driven restructure," CFO says.

item.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: It's not entirely clear how the exploit works. Microsoft says it's investigating.

item.title: In stunning display of stupid, secret CISA credentials found in public GitHub repo (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: SSH keys, plaintext passwords, other sensitive data had been up since November 2025.

item.title: Google publishes exploit code threatening millions of Chromium users (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Google publishes exploit code before patch, reported 42 months earlier, is fixed.

item.title: US government takes $2 billion equity stake in nine quantum computing firms (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Beneficiaries include startup backed by firm with links to the Trump family.

item.title: A hacker group is poisoning open source code at an unprecedented scale (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: GitHub is just the latest victim of TeamPCP, a gang that has carried out a spree of software supply chain attacks.

item.title: Texas AG sues Meta over claims that WhatsApp doesn't provide end-to-end encryption (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Critics note a lack of factual support in lawsuit filed by US Senate candidate.

item.title: US's big bet on quantum computing may not be entirely legal (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Deal also launched the first quantum foundry company, but is there a need for it?

item.title: Millions of AI agents imperiled by critical vulnerability in open source package (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: "BadHost" was found in Starlette, a package with 325 million weekly downloads.

item.title: Websites have a new way to spy on visitors: Analyzing their SSD activity (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Telltale SSD activity can be measured in the browser using simple JavaScript.

item.title: Fed up with vibe coders, dev sneaks data-nuking prompt injection into their code (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Undisclosed addition in jqwik instructed AI coding agents to delete app output.

item.title: Botnet of more than 17 million devices dismantled (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: The botnet was reportedly tied to a Russia-based residential proxy network.

item.title: Dozens of Red Hat packages backdoored through its official NPM channel (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Anyone who has downloaded affected Red Hat packages should investigate immediately.

item.title: Can't make sense of Dashlane's vault theft notification? You're not alone. (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Security advisory leaves out key details. Dashlane maintains complete silence.

item.title: Dashlane explains how attackers managed to download encrypted password vaults (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: By targeting large numbers of users, attackers increased their chances of success.

item.title: How a USB-connected speaker can infect a PC without ever being touched (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Seller of the Sound Blaster Katana V2X doesn't consider the behavior a vulnerability.
